File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f") or SHA1 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f") or MD5 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f") or SHA1 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f") or MD5 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Golden Chickens Resurfaces With Four New Malware Families and Modular Implants

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 16 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actors behind the Golden Chickens malware-as-a-service (MaaS) ecosystem have resurfaced with four new malware families, indicating that the operators are showing no signs of stopping despite extensive public disclosures into their inner workings. The malware families in question are: TinyEgg, ChonkyChicken, a modularized variant of ChonkyChicken, and a modified web browser credential

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TAG-195 ClickFix OCX payload executed via regsvr32 (TinyEgg install) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TAG-195 Golden Chickens C2 beacon to known staging/C2 infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ChromEggscalator: Chromium launched with --remote-debugging-port for cookie/credential theft · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
TAG-195 ClickFix OCX payload executed via regsvr32 (TinyEgg install) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Golden Chickens/TAG-195 delivery signature where a ClickFix Run-dialog paste downloads an OCX and launches it with regsvr32.exe to install the TinyEgg backdoor. Anchored on regsvr32 loading an .ocx / scrobj / remote /i: target from a user-writable directory with a ClickFix-style parent (explorer.exe, cmd.exe, wmic.exe). Rationale: Corroborated by Securonix (OCX#HARVESTER) and Recorded Future: every TAG-195 component ships as an OCX executed via regsvr32.exe after a ClickFix Run-dialog paste. The parent+.ocx/scrobj/user-writable-path combination is the high-fidelity delivery signature, not generic regsvr32. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://www.securonix.com/blog/threat-labs-security-advisory-new-ocxharvester-attack-campaign-leverages-modernized-more_eggs-suite/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/golden-chickens-malware-as-a-service-resurfaces-with-four-new-families
ATT&CKT1218.010 T1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers registering an .ocx ActiveX control (parent msiexec.exe / setup.exe)
  • Admin scripts registering COM controls from a network share via cmd.exe
  • Enterprise deployment tooling (SCCM) invoking regsvr32 from ProgramData
  • Developers re-registering OCX components during build/test
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that self-register controls from AppData on first run
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","ccmexec.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Windows\Installer\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full regsvr32 command line and the parent chain; confirm whether the OCX path is a genuine install dir or a user-writable staging path, and hash the OCX/SHA256 against VT. Check if the parent was explorer.exe (Run-dialog paste = ClickFix). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the regsvr32 process tree, and quarantine the OCX file. 3) Hunt: search the host for follow-on TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken activity — outbound connections to the TAG-195 IOCs, Chrome launched with --remote-debugging-port, and any newly written .ocx modules in AppData/Temp/ProgramData.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "regsvr32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".ocx"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "/i:http"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "scrobj"
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Public\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","cmd.exe","wmic.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\regsvr32.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".ocx" or CommandLine has "/i:http" or CommandLine has "scrobj"
    or CommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Public\")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","cmd.exe","wmic.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TAG-195 OCX Payload Execution via Regsvr32 from User-Writable Path
id: 6f3a1c22-9d4e-4b1a-8c77-1a2b3c4d5e6f
description: Detects Golden Chickens/TAG-195 ClickFix delivery where regsvr32 loads an OCX or remote scrobj target from a user-writable directory, installing the TinyEgg backdoor.
references:
  - https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem
  - https://www.securonix.com/blog/threat-labs-security-advisory-new-ocxharvester-attack-campaign-leverages-modernized-more_eggs-suite/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/30
tags:
  - attack.t1218.010
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\regsvr32.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    - CommandLine|contains: '.ocx'
    - CommandLine|contains: '/i:http'
    - CommandLine|contains: 'scrobj'
    - CommandLine|contains:
        - '\AppData\'
        - '\Temp\'
        - '\ProgramData\'
        - '\Public\'
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\explorer.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\wmic.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd and selection_parent
level: high

TAG-195 Golden Chickens C2 beacon to known staging/C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound connection or resolution to the TAG-195 command-and-control and OCX-staging infrastructure disclosed by Recorded Future. Straight IOC match on the four Vultr-hosted C2 IPs and six campaign domains used by TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken WebSocket C2 and payload staging. Rationale: Direct match on the pre-extracted TAG-195 IPs (Vultr-hosted C2/staging) and campaign domains; these are the concrete network IOCs disclosed in the article and Recorded Future report, high-fidelity while the infrastructure remains live. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/golden-chickens-resurfaces-with-four.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanners / sandbox detonation VMs in the org deliberately reaching the IOCs
  • Security researcher workstation validating the indicators
  • A domain being re-registered/parked and later resolving to benign shared hosting
  • Shared Vultr IP later reassigned to a legitimate tenant (IP reuse) — validate against first-seen date
  • Proxy/URL-filtering appliance logging a block event (connection was denied, not successful)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the host (DeviceNetworkEvents InitiatingProcessFileName) — regsvr32/rundll32/an OCX-hosting process is a strong TinyEgg confirm; note whether the connection succeeded or was blocked. 2) Contain: block all four IPs and six domains at the perimeter and isolate any host with a successful outbound. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash across the fleet, look for the regsvr32/OCX delivery (UC1) and Chrome remote-debugging credential theft (UC3) on the same hosts, and validate IOC freshness before wide blocking.
DeviceNetworkEvents

ChromEggscalator: Chromium launched with --remote-debugging-port for cookie/credential theft AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the ChromEggscalator (ChromElevator-derived) App-Bound Encryption bypass used by ChonkyChicken: a Chromium browser spawned with --remote-debugging-port plus a headless/off-screen or custom user-data-dir flag, typically from a non-browser parent, to drive Chrome DevTools Protocol and steal cookies/passwords. Article-specific to TAG-195's browser-theft module. Rationale: ChromEggscalator is a modified ChromElevator; corroborated by xaitax's GitHub tool and RedCanary, the technique launches Chromium with --remote-debugging-port plus --headless/--window-position (off-screen) or a custom --user-data-dir to drive CDP and dump ABE-protected cookies/passwords — a launch pattern virtually absent from normal user browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://github.com/xaitax/Chrome-App-Bound-Encryption-Decryption • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/google-chrome-app-bound-encryption/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright QA automation launching headless Chrome (parent node.exe/chromedriver.exe)
  • Developers debugging web apps with DevTools remote debugging enabled
  • RPA tooling that drives a headless browser for scraping
  • Automated screenshot/monitoring services (e.g. synthetic checks) launching headless Chromium
  • Browser extension or enterprise-management tooling using a custom --user-data-dir
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe","python.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "--user-data-dir" and ProcessCommandLine has "--headless")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent process and the --remote-debugging-port value; a non-dev parent (regsvr32, rundll32, an OCX host, or an unsigned binary from AppData/Temp) launching headless/off-screen Chrome against the user's real profile dir is a strong ChromEggscalator confirm. 2) Contain: kill the browser+parent process tree, isolate the host, and force-reset the user's browser-synced credentials and session cookies (treat cookies as stolen). 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (regsvr32 OCX install) and UC2 (TAG-195 C2 egress) on the same host, and review recent SSO/session activity for the user for impossible-travel or cookie-replay sign-ins.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","--window-position","--user-data-dir")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\chrome.exe", @"\msedge.exe", @"\brave.exe")
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--headless","--window-position","--user-data-dir")
    or not(ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Chromium Remote Debugging for Browser Credential/Cookie Theft (ChromEggscalator)
id: 9a1e7c34-5d2b-4f80-b6a3-0c1d2e3f4a5b
description: Detects a Chromium browser started with --remote-debugging-port combined with headless/off-screen/custom-profile flags, matching the ChromElevator-derived ChromEggscalator App-Bound Encryption bypass used by TAG-195 ChonkyChicken.
references:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\Brave.exe)) @CommandLine:*--remote-debugging-port* (@CommandLine:*--headless* OR @CommandLine:*--window-position* OR @CommandLine:*--user-data-dir*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/--remote-debugging-port/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chrome.exe OR Processes.process_name=msedge.exe OR Processes.process_name=brave.exe) Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search process="*--headless*" OR process="*--window-position*" OR process="*--user-data-dir*" OR (parent_process_name!=explorer.exe AND parent_process_name!=chrome.exe AND parent_process_name!=msedge.exe AND parent_process_name!=brave.exe AND parent_process_name!=userinit.exe) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/

            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1204.002

    category: process_creation

            - '\explorer.exe'

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")

        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] msaRAT: curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Don’t swing at everything

msaRAT: MSI impersonating Windows update executed from ProgramData AIInstallation High
Hunts msiexec.exe executing an MSI dropped to C:\ProgramData whose name/property info impersonates a Windows update, matching Chaos ransomware's msaRAT delivery where a custom action loads the RAT DLL straight into memory. Article-specific: the installer masquerades as a Windows update and lives in ProgramData rather than a signed update path. Rationale: Uses the article's exact delivery: an MSI in ProgramData impersonating a Windows update executed by msiexec, with a memory-loading custom action. Cross-checked against Talos full report and The Hacker News which confirm the installer property info impersonates a Windows update. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party software packaged as an MSI staged in ProgramData by a legitimate installer bootstrapper
  • Enterprise software distribution (SCCM/Intune) caching update MSIs under ProgramData vendor folders
  • Driver/firmware update utilities (Dell, Lenovo, HP) that stage MSIs named with 'Update' in ProgramData
  • Legitimate Windows optional-feature MSIs referenced with KB numbers in command line
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full msiexec command line and the MSI file hash; check the parent process and whether the MSI is signed and by whom (msaRAT installer is unsigned/impersonates Windows). Query DeviceImageLoadEvents for a DLL loaded by msiexec.exe from ProgramData at the same time. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, kill the msiexec/child process tree, and block the MSI hash org-wide. 3) Hunt: Look on the same host for a preceding curl.exe download to ProgramData and subsequent headless chrome.exe/msedge.exe launched with --remote-debugging flags (msaRAT CDP C2).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\ProgramData\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","kb","patch","windows")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "\\ProgramData\\"
| where CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has_any ("update","kb","patch","windows")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT MSI Impersonating Windows Update from ProgramData

msaRAT: curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData AIDelivery High
Detects curl.exe (or wget) retrieving a .msi to C:\ProgramData, the exact ingress step Talos describes for Chaos ransomware's msaRAT before the fake Windows-update installer runs. Article-specific: correlates the curl download with the msaRAT delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the workers.dev signaling infra. Rationale: Directly implements Talos's 'monitor for unusual curl commands downloading MSI files to ProgramData' guidance, anchored on the confirmed delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the workers.dev signaling domain. Corroborated by The Hacker News and Help Net Security. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or DevOps scripts using curl to fetch MSI installers into a working directory under ProgramData
  • Software packaging/CI agents downloading MSI artifacts to a ProgramData staging cache
  • Admin manually fetching a vendor MSI with curl for testing
  • Chocolatey/winget-style tooling that shells out to curl for package retrieval
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("choco.exe","winget.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "workers.dev" == false)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Extract the full download URL from the curl command line and check reputation of the host/IP; confirm the destination path in ProgramData and whether the resulting MSI was subsequently executed by msiexec. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, block the URL/IP (172.86.126.18) and workers.dev signaling domain at proxy/firewall, and quarantine the downloaded MSI. 3) Hunt: Search the host and org for the same URL/IP in DeviceNetworkEvents and for a following headless browser launch with --remote-debugging (msaRAT C2 stage).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\ProgramData\" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("172.86.126.18","workers.dev")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wget.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has "\\ProgramData\\" or CommandLine has_any ("172.86.126.18","workers.dev")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT: Headless Chrome/Edge launched with remote-debugging (CDP abuse) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts chrome.exe/msedge.exe spawned with --remote-debugging-port/--remote-debugging-pipe (and typically --headless) by a non-interactive parent, the mechanism msaRAT uses to drive a browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol for covert C2. Article-specific: the RAT starts its own headless browser instance and controls it via CDP rather than touching the network directly. Rationale: Targets the CDP-driven headless browser msaRAT spawns for C2 (Talos: 'implement behavioral monitoring to catch Chrome DevTools Protocol abuse'). Confirmed by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News that the RAT starts Chrome/Edge in headless mode and drives it over CDP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1205 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated browser testing frameworks (Puppeteer, Playwright, Selenium headless) run by developers or CI runners
  • PDF-generation or web-scraping services that drive headless Chromium
  • Lighthouse/synthetic-monitoring agents launching headless Edge/Chrome
  • Electron-based apps invoking a bundled Chromium with debugging pipe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","lighthouse"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the parent process that launched the headless browser and its binary path/signature; a browser started by an unsigned/unknown parent (not a dev tool, IDE, or CI agent) is high-suspicion. Check for a co-occurring loopback (127.0.0.1) debugging listener. 2) Contain: If the parent is untrusted, isolate the host and kill the browser + parent tree. 3) Hunt: Pivot from the host to DeviceNetworkEvents for browser egress to workers.dev / STUN (3478) / Twilio TURN, and back to any preceding msiexec-from-ProgramData execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend Headless = ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where Headless or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","userinit.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Headless, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend Headless = CommandLine has "--headless"
| where Headless or ParentProcessName !endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, Headless, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Headless Browser Launched with Remote Debugging (msaRAT CDP C2)
id: b1e6f4a2-9c3d-4a7e-8b21-5d0c7e9a1f33
description: chrome.exe/msedge.exe started with remote-debugging flags in headless mode - Chrome DevTools Protocol abuse used by Chaos ransomware msaRAT for covert C2
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:
  - attack.t1205
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--remote-debugging-port'
      - '--remote-debugging-pipe'
  selection_headless:
    CommandLine|contains: '--headless'
  condition: selection and selection_headless
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MsEdge.exe OR *\MSEDGE.EXE) @CommandLine:(*--remote-debugging-port* OR *--remote-debugging-pipe*) @CommandLine:*--headless*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/--remote-debugging-(port|pipe)/i
| CommandLine=/--headless/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN (chrome.exe,msedge.exe) (Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" OR Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-pipe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search parent_process_name!=explorer.exe parent_process_name!=chrome.exe parent_process_name!=msedge.exe | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN (chrome.exe,msedge.exe) (Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" OR Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-pipe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search parent_process_name!=explorer.exe parent_process_name!=chrome.exe parent_process_name!=msedge.exe | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
msaRAT: Connection to Chaos delivery IP / workers.dev signaling relay AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the msaRAT delivery server 172.86.126.18 (plain HTTP over port 443) or the Cloudflare workers.dev signaling relay is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev. Article-specific: these are the confirmed network IOCs for msaRAT's payload delivery and WebRTC signaling. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the confirmed msaRAT delivery server (172.86.126.18, plain HTTP over 443) and the workers.dev signaling relay, both published in the Talos report and echoed by Security Affairs/Help Net Security. High-fidelity, low-FP IOC alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195876/malware/chaos-ransomware-deploys-browser-based-msarat-to-evade-network-detection.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign traffic to an unrelated tenant sharing the ols-img-12.workers.dev Cloudflare Worker subdomain (unlikely but possible if the subdomain is later repurposed)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the sample and generating IOC contact from a research host
  • Threat-intel enrichment or IOC-validation scanners in the environment reaching the IP
  • Stale IOC after infrastructure takedown produces sinkhole hits
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process — a browser (chrome/msedge) reaching workers.dev or any process reaching 172.86.126.18 on 443; confirm whether traffic to the IP is plain HTTP despite the 443 port (protocol mismatch is a strong indicator). 2) Contain: Block the IP and domain at the perimeter, isolate the host, and capture the process tree. 3) Hunt: On the host, look for the preceding curl→ProgramData MSI download, msiexec fake-update execution, and a headless browser launched with --remote-debugging; sweep the org for any other host that contacted either IOC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18" or RemoteUrl =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "172.86.126.18" or DstHostname =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or Url has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT: Headless browser initiating WebRTC STUN/TURN egress AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts chrome.exe/msedge.exe making STUN/TURN connections (ports 3478/5349) when the browser was launched non-interactively with debugging/headless flags — the WebRTC data-channel egress msaRAT relays through Twilio TURN for C2. Article-specific: msaRAT sends a STUN request then tunnels C2 over WebRTC from its own headless browser, not user-driven WebRTC. Rationale: Targets msaRAT's WebRTC egress (STUN request + Twilio TURN relay) constrained to a headless/CDP-driven browser so it isn't just generic WebRTC noise. Talos, BleepingComputer and The Hacker News confirm the STUN-then-WebRTC-via-Twilio C2 path. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate video conferencing / VoIP in-browser (Google Meet, Teams web, Discord web) using WebRTC STUN/TURN
  • Browser-based screen-sharing or WebRTC test pages initiated by a user
  • Puppeteer/Playwright automation that legitimately exercises WebRTC
  • Corporate SBC/collaboration platforms relaying media over 3478/5349
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("teams.exe","ms-teams.exe","slack.exe","discord.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the browser was launched non-interactively (parent is not explorer.exe and command line carries --headless/--remote-debugging); user-driven Meet/Teams WebRTC will have an interactive parent and no debugging flags. 2) Contain: If non-interactive, isolate the host, kill the browser + parent, and block the TURN destination and the workers.dev signaling domain. 3) Hunt: Correlate on the host with the CDP browser-launch detection, contact to 172.86.126.18 / workers.dev, and the fake-update MSI chain; check for Chaos ransomware staging (shadow-copy deletion, RMM tools).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where RemotePort in (3478, 5349)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstPortNumber in (3478, 5349)
| where NetworkProtocol has_any ("UDP","TCP")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-23 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

In the second quarter of 2026, the continuing effects of Microsoft’s disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing platform contributed to sustained declines in several major phishing techniques, while threat actors expanded into Teams-based social engineering and employed increasingly automated and multi-stage attack chains. The post Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound phishing from BEC sender domain 9i6pokerdepot.com (Q2 2026 ClickUp/pixeldrain chain) · [LLM] Financial_report.bat dropper downloaded from ClickUp attachment host · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Hidden PowerShell pulls installer.exe from pixeldrain.com to %Temp% (self-deleting dropper) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network/DNS contact to Q2 2026 campaign infrastructure (pixeldrain payload + ClickUp dropper hosts) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Inbound phishing from BEC sender domain 9i6pokerdepot.com (Q2 2026 ClickUp/pixeldrain chain) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound email from the DKIM-signed operator domain 9i6pokerdepot.com (sender Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com) used in Microsoft's Q2 2026 multi-stage campaign that lured users with a fake 'Internal Affairs – Financials & Staff Updates' message. This is the delivery anchor of the chain that ends in silent malware execution via ClickUp and pixeldrain. Rationale: Anchors on the exact sender domain (9i6pokerdepot.com) and full address (Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com) from the article's IOC table; a niche gambling-themed domain sending to enterprise mailboxes is effectively zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1656
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security team deliberately replays the IOC domain in a phishing-simulation/purple-team exercise
  • Threat-intel or sandbox tooling that re-sends captured campaign samples into a test mailbox
  • A researcher forwarding the original email internally for analysis (appears as intra-org, not inbound)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all recipients of the message via NetworkMessageId; check DeliveryLocation (Inbox vs Quarantine) and whether any user opened it. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide with an EmailPostDelivery/ZAP action and block 9i6pokerdepot.com at the mail gateway and Safe Links. 3) Hunt: for every recipient, pivot to UC2/UC3 — look for Financial_report.bat writes and PowerShell contacting pixeldrain.com on their devices in the following 24h.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email where All_Email.direction="inbound" AND (All_Email.src_user="Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com" OR All_Email.src_user="*@9i6pokerdepot.com") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.message_id | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email where All_Email.direction="inbound" AND (All_Email.src_user="Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com" OR All_Email.src_user="*@9i6pokerdepot.com") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.message_id | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Financial_report.bat dropper downloaded from ClickUp attachment host AIDelivery High
Detects the stage-2 batch dropper (Financial_report.bat) written to disk with a download origin of clickup-attachments.com — the trusted-service hop the Q2 2026 campaign used after a login.microsoftonline.com redirect. ClickUp's public attachment host serving a .bat file is the article-specific tell. Rationale: Uses the exact dropper filename (Financial_report.bat) and the trusted-service host (clickup-attachments.com, subdomain t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com) from the article and corroborating write-up; a .bat sourced from ClickUp is not a legitimate business pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/
ATT&CKT1105 T1608.001 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A dev team legitimately storing build/automation .bat scripts as ClickUp task attachments and downloading them
  • IR/malware analyst intentionally downloading the sample from ClickUp for analysis
  • Generic '.bat in %Temp%' branch firing on an installer's own temporary batch helper (mitigated by the clickup-attachments.com origin clause on the primary path)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","outlook.exe","explorer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged host, capture the SHA256 of Financial_report.bat and the InitiatingProcess (browser/Outlook) that wrote it; confirm the FileOriginUrl subdomain. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the .bat already executed (check for cmd.exe→powershell.exe children); block clickup-attachments.com download paths at proxy and delete the file. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 — search DeviceProcessEvents on the same host/user for PowerShell referencing pixeldrain.com and installer.exe in %Temp%.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileOriginUrl has "clickup-attachments.com"
| where FileName =~ "Financial_report.bat" or FileName endswith ".bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "clickup-attachments.com"
| where FileName endswith ".bat" or Url has "Financial_report.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, FileName, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
